quick_summary: Two-dimensional projectile motion is analyzed by resolving vectors into independent horizontal and vertical components. With air resistance neglected, gravity produces constant downward acceleration, horizontal velocity remains constant, the trajectory is parabolic, and collision or maximum-height conditions follow from the component equations.

key_concepts.explanation: Position, velocity, and acceleration in two dimensions are represented as x- and y-components: r(t)=x(t)î+y(t)ĵ, with velocity and acceleration obtained by differentiating component-wise.
An initial speed v₀ launched at angle θ₀ has components vₓ,₀=v₀ cosθ₀ and vᵧ,₀=v₀ sinθ₀.
When air resistance and other interactions are neglected, the only force is gravity, Fg=−mg ĵ, giving aᵧ=−g and aₓ=0.
Integrating the constant accelerations gives vₓ=vₓ,₀, x=x₀+vₓ,₀t, vᵧ=vᵧ,₀−gt, and y=y₀+vᵧ,₀t−½gt².
At the highest point, the vertical velocity is zero. Thus ttop=v₀ sinθ₀/g, and the maximum height is y₀+v₀² sin²θ₀/(2g).
Eliminating time between x(t) and y(t) produces a quadratic y(x), so ideal projectile motion follows a parabola.
The slope dy/dx equals vᵧ/vₓ and determines the direction angle of the velocity vector, but the geometric orbit alone does not determine the speed.

For a ball aimed at a simultaneously released pail, matching horizontal and vertical positions shows θ₀=tan⁻¹((h₁−h₂)/s), independent of launch speed; collision time decreases as launch speed increases.

relationships.target: Vertical velocity decrease linearly with time
Actual trajectory to differ from ideal parabolic trajectory

visual_evidence.learning_value: Contrasts the ideal model with its limitation and connects x-y coordinates to the projectile’s vector position.

visual_evidence.description: Figure 5.3 decomposes the initial velocity vector into horizontal and vertical components.
visual_evidence.learning_value: Makes the trigonometric component relations vₓ,₀=v₀cosθ₀ and vᵧ,₀=v₀sinθ₀ visually concrete.

visual_evidence.description: Figure 5.4 is a free-body diagram showing gravity acting downward.
visual_evidence.learning_value: Directly supports the conclusion that acceleration is vertical and downward.

visual_evidence.description: Figures 5.5 and 5.6 show the parabolic path y(x) and the vertical position y(t) for the worked stone example.
visual_evidence.learning_value: Distinguishes spatial trajectory from time evolution and illustrates how graph slope represents velocity.

visual_evidence.description: Figure 5.7 plots vertical velocity vᵧ(t) as a decreasing straight line crossing zero at the highest point.
visual_evidence.learning_value: Shows why vᵧ=0 identifies maximum height and why the sign change marks the transition from ascent to descent.

visual_evidence.description: Figure 5.8 depicts the parabolic orbit with velocity components and the local tangent direction.
visual_evidence.learning_value: Connects the orbit’s tangent slope with the instantaneous velocity direction.

visual_evidence.description: Figure 5.9 illustrates the falling-pail and thrown-ball setup, including h₁, h₂, and horizontal separation s.
visual_evidence.learning_value: Frames the simultaneous-motion collision problem geometrically.

visual_flow.reason: The central idea is an ordered derivation: specify initial components, apply the gravity-only force model, integrate acceleration, obtain the trajectory, and impose conditions for features such as maximum height or collision.

concept_map.reason: A process flow better represents the chapter’s main derivation than a static conceptual map.

comparison.reason: The material includes contrasts such as ideal versus air-resisted motion, but comparison is not its dominant learning structure.

learning_path.title: From Vector Components to Projectile Outcomes
learning_path.reason: The chapter develops projectile motion through a clear mathematical progression from representation and forces to equations, geometry, and applications.

steps.title: Represent motion with components
steps.learning_goal: Express position, velocity, and acceleration in Cartesian components.
steps.explanation: Treat x and y independently: r=x î+y ĵ, v=vₓ î+vᵧ ĵ, and a=aₓ î+aᵧ ĵ. Resolve the launch velocity using the speed and angle.
steps.connection_to_previous: This establishes the language needed to analyze motion in two dimensions.

steps.title: Translate gravity into acceleration
steps.learning_goal: Derive the horizontal and vertical accelerations for ideal projectile motion.
steps.explanation: The gravity force is downward, Fg=−mg ĵ. Newton’s second law gives aₓ=0 and aᵧ=−g, independent of the projectile’s mass.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once the components are defined, the force model determines how each component changes.

steps.title: Integrate to obtain x(t), y(t), and velocity
steps.learning_goal: Use the constant accelerations to write the complete time-dependent motion.
steps.explanation: Horizontal motion is uniform: x=x₀+vₓ,₀t. Vertical motion is uniformly accelerated: y=y₀+vᵧ,₀t−½gt² and vᵧ=vᵧ,₀−gt.
steps.connection_to_previous: Integrating the accelerations produces the position and velocity functions that describe the flight.

steps.title: Interpret the trajectory geometrically
steps.learning_goal: Understand why the path is parabolic and how its slope relates to velocity direction.
steps.explanation: Eliminating t gives a quadratic y(x). The slope dy/dx=vᵧ/vₓ determines the direction of motion at a point, while the graph alone does not determine speed.
steps.connection_to_previous: The time equations can be combined to describe the path without using time explicitly.

steps.title: Solve special-event problems
steps.learning_goal: Apply physical conditions to find maximum height and collision results.
steps.explanation: At maximum height vᵧ=0. For the falling-pail problem, require the ball and pail to share x and y at the same time, yielding θ₀=tan⁻¹((h₁−h₂)/s) and tₐ=√(s²+(h₁−h₂)²)/v₀.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once the trajectory and velocity are known, physical events are found by imposing their defining conditions.

checkpoint_questions.question: A projectile is launched with speed v₀ at angle θ₀. Which pair gives its initial velocity components?
checkpoint_questions.explanation: The horizontal component is adjacent to θ₀ and the vertical component is opposite, so vₓ,₀=v₀cosθ₀ and vᵧ,₀=v₀sinθ₀.

checkpoint_questions.question: Why is the vertical velocity zero at the projectile’s highest point?

options.text: The vertical position stops increasing before it begins decreasing
The projectile has no acceleration at that point

checkpoint_questions.explanation: At the apex, y(t) changes from increasing to decreasing, so its slope dy/dt=vᵧ is zero; gravity still acts downward.

checkpoint_questions.question: In the falling-pail problem, why does the required aiming angle not depend on the ball’s initial speed?

options.text: Both objects experience the same downward acceleration, which cancels when their position conditions are compared
The ball has no vertical velocity
The pail remains fixed horizontally because gravity is absent
The collision time is always independent of speed

checkpoint_questions.explanation: The ball and pail share the same gravitational acceleration, so comparing their vertical positions leaves v₀ only in factors that cancel when the horizontal and vertical conditions are divided.

interactive_lab.reason: The source provides an explicit projectile orbit equation whose shape and maximum height become clearer when launch speed, angle, and release height are varied.

demos.learning_goal: See how launch speed, launch angle, and initial height change the parabolic path and the time to maximum height.
